ordered_diagnoses: Spinal cord compression due to metastasis

facts.raw_span: A 50-year-old man
no significant past medical history
1-week history of rapidly progressive gait disturbance
no back pain, fevers, night sweats, or weight loss
full strength throughout all extremities
decreased sensation from the T3 dermatome downward
four beats of clonus bilaterally
hyperreflexia in the lower extremities
profound ataxia, rendering him unable to walk more than a few steps
Contrast-enhanced MRI of the thoracic spine demonstrated a diffusely enhancing lesion centered at T1 with near-circumferential epidural extension causing severe cord compression
CT of the thoracic spine showed an expansile bony lesion of the T1 vertebral body with extension into the left pedicle and posterior elements
CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed no evidence of a primary malignancy

concepts.preferred_label: Spinal cord compression due to metastasis
concepts.why: The patient's rapidly progressive gait disturbance and decreased sensation from the T3 dermatome downward, along with the imaging findings of a diffusely enhancing lesion centered at T1 with near-circumferential epidural extension causing severe cord compression, suggest spinal cord compression due to metastasis.

The patient's imaging findings of an expansile bony lesion of the T1 vertebral body with extension into the left pedicle and posterior elements, along with the absence of a primary malignancy, could suggest hematogenous osteomyelitis.

The patient's rapidly progressive neurological decline, decreased sensation from the T3 dermatome downward, and imaging findings of a diffusely enhancing lesion centered at T1 with near-circumferential epidural extension, could suggest a spinal epidural abscess.

The patient's imaging findings of an expansile bony lesion of the T1 vertebral body with extension into the left pedicle and posterior elements, along with the absence of a primary malignancy, could suggest multiple myeloma.

The patient's imaging findings of a diffusely enhancing lesion centered at T1 with near-circumferential epidural extension causing severe cord compression, along with the absence of a primary malignancy, could suggest lymphoma.

The patient's imaging findings of an expansile bony lesion of the T1 vertebral body with extension into the left pedicle and posterior elements, along with the absence of a primary malignancy, could suggest chordoma.

The patient's imaging findings of an expansile bony lesion of the T1 vertebral body with extension into the left pedicle and posterior elements, along with the absence of a primary malignancy, could suggest plasmacytoma.

The patient's imaging findings of an expansile bony lesion of the T1 vertebral body with extension into the left pedicle and posterior elements, along with the absence of a primary malignancy, could suggest Ewing's sarcoma.

The patient's imaging findings of an expansile bony lesion of the T1 vertebral body with extension into the left pedicle and posterior elements, along with the absence of a primary malignancy, could suggest osteosarcoma.

The patient's imaging findings of an expansile bony lesion of the T1 vertebral body with extension into the left pedicle and posterior elements, along with the absence of a primary malignancy, could suggest chondrosarcoma.

rationales.F11: Expansile bony lesion with extension into pedicle and posterior elements is highly suggestive of spinal cord compression due to metastasis
